young.html: Bertolt Brecht was a German playwright. He wanted plays to make people think, not just cry. So his plays have songs, signs that tell you what will happen next, and characters who sometimes seem to talk right to the audience.

Mother Courage and Her Children takes place long ago, during a war that lasted thirty years. Mother Courage pulls a wagon full of things to sell to soldiers: boots, bread, brandy and belts. She thinks the war is good for business, and she hopes to keep her three grown children safe and earn a living from it at the same time. But the war takes all three of them, one by one. Her brave daughter Kattrin, who cannot speak, saves a whole town by beating a drum to warn them.
For parents: the play is about war's cost to a family; all three children die, which the lesson mentions without detail. Best for teens and adults.

young.html: Make a sign. Brecht hung signs before each scene saying what would happen, so the audience would watch how and why, not just what. Pick a fairy tale and write a sign for each part ("Scene 1: The wolf meets a girl in the woods"). Then act it with the signs. Does knowing what's coming change what you notice?

full.html: Bertolt Brecht (1898–1956) was born in Augsburg, Bavaria, and made his name in 1920s Berlin with The Threepenny Opera (1928), written with the composer Kurt Weill. A Marxist, he fled Germany when the Nazis came to power in 1933 and lived in exile in Denmark, Sweden, Finland and the United States. He wrote Mother Courage in Sweden in 1939, as the Second World War began. It was first staged in Zurich in 1941. After the war he founded the Berliner Ensemble in East Berlin, where his wife, the actress Helene Weigel, played Mother Courage.
About quotations: the play was first published after 1930 and is still under copyright, so this lesson describes it in our own words. See "Read the full text" above for where to find it.

The twelve scenes run from 1624 to 1636, in the middle of the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648), which began as a religious conflict between Catholic and Protestant states and grew into a European struggle for power that devastated the German lands. Anna Fierling, called Mother Courage, follows the armies of both sides with her canteen wagon. She has three children by different fathers: Eilif, bold; Swiss Cheese, honest; and Kattrin, kind, who cannot speak.

Each child is undone by a virtue the war turns into a danger. Eilif's daring wins praise in war, but when he does the same thing during a brief peace he is executed. Swiss Cheese's honesty leads him to hide his regiment's cash box, and he is shot while his mother haggles over the bribe that could have saved him. Kattrin's compassion makes her climb a roof and drum to warn a sleeping town of a surprise attack; she saves the town and is killed. At the end Courage, alone, harnesses herself to her wagon and follows the army again.

full.html: Brecht called his method "epic theater." Signs, songs and a deliberately un-magical stage keep the audience at a thinking distance (his "estrangement" or "alienation" effect), so that they judge Courage rather than simply pity her. He wanted them to see that she lives off the war that destroys her family, and never learns.

Audiences often wept for Courage anyway, and admired her toughness. Brecht revised the play to make her less sympathetic. Whether she is a victim, a villain or both is still argued; the play's power may come from that tension.

Calling the play a story of heroism, as the name "Courage" suggests. She got the nickname, the play says, for driving her wagon through a bombardment to sell bread before it went moldy: courage for the sake of business.

items: Grimmelshausen's 17th-century novels of the Thirty Years' War, including one about a camp follower named Courasche, gave Brecht his heroine's name and world.
Euripides' Trojan Women, on this ladder's Greek rungs, also shows war through the women it leaves behind.
Aristotle's Poetics said tragedy works through pity and fear; Brecht set out to replace that with critical thinking.
Tolstoy's War and Peace and Thucydides, earlier on this ladder, are other great portraits of war's cost.
Can a person profit from a war without sharing its blame?
Why do the children's virtues, bravery, honesty and kindness, put them in danger?
Should a play make us feel, or make us think? Can it do both?
Why does Courage never seem to learn?

questions: Mother Courage loved her children and also loved her business. When did those two loves clash?
Kattrin couldn't speak, but she saved a town. What gave her the courage?
Why do you think Brecht put up signs telling the audience what would happen?
Is "Mother Courage" a good name for her? Why or why not?
What does war do to ordinary families, in this play and in history you know?
